title: Willing Gifts, David's Prayer, and Solomon Enthroned
summary: David gives his own treasure for the temple and invites the leaders to give, and they respond freely and joyfully. David blesses the LORD in a great prayer that confesses everything as God's gift, the assembly worships and feasts, and Solomon is anointed king a second time. The chapter, and the book, closes with a summary of David's forty-year reign and his death.
story: This is the last scene of First Chronicles and the completion of the handover begun in chapter 28. David has given Solomon the plan and the charge; now he gives the materials, and the nation joins him. The chapter moves from giving to praise to coronation, and ends with David's death. The Chronicler has spent most of his account of David on the ark, the temple, and the ordering of worship, and he closes it on the same note: David's last public act is an offering and a prayer. Second Chronicles will open with Solomon firmly established and ready to build.
historical:
The scene is set around 970 BC at the end of David's reign. The summary in verses 26 to 30 agrees with 1 Kings 2:10-11 on the forty-year reign, seven years at Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. Verse 22 says Solomon was made king “a second time”, which looks back to 1 Chronicles 23:1, where David, old and full of days, made Solomon king. First Kings 1 tells of a hurried anointing at the Gihon spring in response to Adonijah's attempt to take the throne; the Chronicler presents a public, joyful confirmation.

Verse 7 mentions darics, a Persian gold coin named for or associated with Darius I and first minted around the end of the sixth century BC, some five centuries after David. The Chronicler is almost certainly converting the gift into the currency his readers knew, in the way a modern writer might give an ancient sum in dollars. It is one of the clearest signs that Chronicles was written in the Persian period. Verse 29 names the prophetic records of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad as sources for David's reign, writings that have not survived as separate books.
cultural:
Giving to a temple was common across the ancient world, and kings in particular boasted of the gold and silver they lavished on their gods' houses. What stands out here is the emphasis on willingness. The Hebrew verb nadav (to give freely, to volunteer) appears again and again, and the people's joy comes not from the size of the gifts but from the fact that they were given freely and wholeheartedly (verse 9). The model is the tabernacle offering in Exodus 35 and 36, where the people brought so much willingly that Moses had to tell them to stop.

The amounts are vast. A talent was a heavy unit of weight, often estimated at roughly 30 kilograms, so thousands of talents would be an enormous treasure. Gold of Ophir was proverbial for its quality, though Ophir's location is unknown; southern Arabia, the East African coast, and India have all been proposed. The thousand bulls, rams, and lambs of verse 21 were burnt offerings, wholly consumed on the altar, but the verse adds other sacrifices in abundance, most likely fellowship offerings whose meat was eaten by the worshipers, which is why the day ends with eating and drinking “with great joy in the presence of the LORD” (verse 22).
literary: The chapter has four movements: David's appeal and the people's response (verses 1 to 9), David's prayer (10 to 19), the assembly's worship and Solomon's coronation (20 to 25), and the closing notice on David's reign (26 to 30). The prayer is the heart of it. It opens with a doxology, a hymn of praise piling up words for God's greatness, then turns to humble confession (“who am I”), to the brevity of human life, and finally to intercession for the people and for Solomon. The key words are repeated deliberately: give, willing, heart, and hand. The book ends with a formal source citation, a habit the Chronicler shares with the books of Kings.

outline.t: David's gifts and his appeal to the leaders
The leaders give willingly and the people rejoice
David blesses the LORD and prays for his people and his son
Worship, sacrifice, and Solomon anointed king
The summary of David's reign and his death

doctrines.note: David's prayer confesses that “everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You” and that God is “the ruler over all” (verses 11-12). Riches, honor, and strength are gifts from his hand. Even Israel's giving is only returning what God first gave (verse 14).

The prayer models the shape of biblical praise: adoration first, then confession of human smallness, then petition. David asks not for more wealth but that God would keep the people's hearts directed toward him and give Solomon a whole heart to obey (verses 18-19).

“Our days on earth are like a shadow, without hope” (verse 15). At the height of his wealth and success, David confesses that human beings are passing guests in God's world. The generous heart and the humble heart turn out to be the same heart.

words.note: Nadav, to be willing, to offer freely, to volunteer. It is used seven times in this chapter, and it is the chapter's theme. The same root gives the noun for a freewill offering. God is honored not by what is extracted but by what is given freely.

Levav, heart, the inner self where thought, will, and desire meet. David prays with an “upright heart” (verse 17) and asks God to direct the people's hearts and give Solomon a “whole heart” (verse 19). In Hebrew thought the heart is less the seat of emotion than of intention and decision.

Ger, a sojourner or resident foreigner, someone living in a land not his own and without the full rights of a native. David uses it, with its partner word toshav, to describe Israel before God: “we are foreigners and strangers in Your presence, as were all our forefathers” (verse 15), recalling Abraham's life as a sojourner in Canaan.

Barakh, to bless. When God blesses people he gives them life and good; when people bless God, as here (verses 10 and 20), they praise him and acknowledge him as the source of every good. The chapter turns on this reversal: God has blessed Israel, and Israel blesses God.

christ: David's doxology in verse 11 has had a long life in Christian worship. Many scholars think the familiar ending of the Lord's Prayer, the kingdom and the power and the glory, which appears in later manuscripts of Matthew 6:13 and in early Christian worship, echoes this verse. Solomon sitting “on the throne of the LORD” (verse 23) is one of the Chronicler's boldest phrases: the son of David rules on God's own throne. The New Testament presents Jesus, the son of David, as raised and seated at God's right hand, ruling with the authority that Solomon only foreshadowed. And David's confession that his people are strangers and sojourners is picked up by Hebrews 11:13, which describes the patriarchs as confessing that they were strangers and exiles on the earth, looking for a better country. The link is thematic: the New Testament sees in Christ both the king David's line was waiting for and the homeland his pilgrims were seeking.

hard.q: Can the enormous amounts of gold and silver in this chapter be historical?
hard.a:
Taken at face value, the thousands of talents in verses 4 and 7 (together with the 100,000 talents of gold in 1 Chronicles 22:14) amount to hundreds or thousands of tonnes of precious metal, far beyond what a small kingdom in the tenth century BC is likely to have held. Interpreters respond in several ways. Some think the figures are accurate and reflect David's plunder from his many wars, noting that ancient royal inscriptions do record huge tributes. Others suggest that the value of the talent may have differed from later standards, or that numbers have been enlarged in the course of copying, a known feature of numbers in ancient manuscripts. Many see the figures as deliberately grand, a way of expressing the glory of the temple and the generosity of its builders in the most splendid terms available, much as the daric in verse 7 translates the gift into the reader's own currency.

Whatever view one takes, the chapter's point doesn't depend on the exact sums. David himself says that all of it came from God's hand, and that what pleases God is uprightness of heart and willing giving (verse 17).

questions: David says, “from Your own hand we have given to You” (verse 14). How would it change your giving to see it as returning rather than surrendering?
The people rejoiced because their leaders gave freely. How does the example of leaders shape the generosity of a community?
At the height of his success David calls human life a shadow. Why might it be important to remember our frailty especially when things are going well?
